change-story.name: Change Story
change-story.summary: A change management narrative that addresses the emotional and rational objections employees face when asked to change.
change-story.description: A change management narrative that addresses the emotional and rational objections people face when asked to change. Establish the burning platform, explain why the timing is urgent, show the chosen path and the alternatives it was chosen over, make the stakes concrete for the organization, the team, and individuals, and close on a shared vision in which the audience is the protagonist. The tone is motivational and empathetic: it acknowledges that change is hard while building conviction. Best for organizational change, transformation announcements, restructuring communications, and all-hands meetings; typical decks run 8-15 slides.

beats.name: Why Change
beats.description: Acknowledge the current state and the external or internal forces requiring change. Don't skip the burning platform.
beats.instructions: Explain why the current state cannot continue.

beats.name: Why Now
beats.description: Explain the urgency. What changes if we wait? What window is closing?
beats.instructions: Make the timing urgent and concrete.

beats.name: Why This Way
beats.description: Show that alternatives were considered. Build trust by demonstrating thoughtful decision-making.
beats.instructions: Describe the proposed path and why it fits.

beats.name: What's at Stake
beats.description: Make consequences concrete for the organization, the team, and individuals. Avoid abstract language.
beats.instructions: Show the risks and rewards attached to the choice.

beats.name: How We Win Together
beats.description: Paint a shared vision of success. Make the audience the protagonist of the new story.
beats.instructions: Close with shared ownership and first commitments.

engineering-team.name: Engineering Team
engineering-team.summary: Practitioners building the system; they want depth, mechanism, and tradeoffs.
engineering-team.description: Engineers tune out generalities and tune in to specifics. Show benchmarks with conditions, architecture diagrams with constraints, and tradeoffs you actually considered. Internal jargon is fine — assume the room shares it. Leave room for questions; engineering audiences engage best when they can poke at the proposal.

investor.name: Investor
investor.summary: Angel investors, VCs, or institutional investors evaluating financial viability, market opportunity, and team.
investor.description: Angel, venture, and institutional investors judging financial viability, market opportunity, and the team. Lead with traction, size the market (TAM, SAM, SOM), make the moat and differentiation explicit, and show financial projections with their assumptions stated. Moderate chart density; 12-20 slides.

pitch.name: Pitch
pitch.summary: Present an opportunity and ask for investment, approval, partnership, or sponsorship.
pitch.description: Use when the deck needs to create interest and move a high-stakes audience toward backing the opportunity. Lead with the opportunity, prove credibility, and make the ask concrete.
pitch.outcome: The audience agrees to invest, sponsor, approve, or continue the conversation.
successCriteria: Ask and next step are explicit

persuasive.name: Persuasive
persuasive.summary: Argument-led voice for sales, fundraising, and recommendation-driven decks.
persuasive.description: Frame every section as an argument that builds toward an ask. Surface objections, answer them, and pair claims with the strongest available proof. Read more like a memo than a report.
voiceCues: Lead each section with the claim it's making.
Surface the strongest counter-argument and address it.
Pair every claim with proof — customer, benchmark, or analyst.
End on a clear ask with named owner and date.
avoid: Symmetrical 'on one hand / on the other' framing without a verdict.
Information for its own sake — every chart should advance the argument.
Passive endings without a clear ask.
samplePhrases: Adopting our runtime cuts inference latency 8× while preserving accuracy.
The most common objection — 'we'll be locked in' — is addressed by our open OPF spec.
We're asking for a $30M Series B to ship into the enterprise tier.

cover.name: Cover
cover.summary: The opening slide: title, subtitle and an optional picture.
cover.description: Open a presentation with its subject and a short introduction. Add a picture when it helps establish the context.

text.name: Text
text.summary: Prose. Several blocks sit side by side when short and stack when long.
text.description: Explain one idea in continuous prose. Use paragraphs or flowing blocks for detail that needs to be read in sequence.

chart.name: Chart
chart.summary: One to six charts, with an optional note.
chart.description: Give a chart enough space to show its evidence. Use the title to state the conclusion and labels to explain the measures.

table-beside.name: Table beside
table-beside.summary: A table with commentary beside it.
table-beside.description: Place a table beside its interpretation. Use the supporting text to explain the conclusion without repeating every cell.

timeline.name: Timeline
timeline.summary: Dated events or a roadmap along one axis, with optional notes.
timeline.description: Show events or milestones in chronological order. Label each item with a date or stage and a concise description.

list.name: List
list.summary: Bulleted or numbered points; one long list flows into columns.
list.description: Present several related points in a clear sequence. Use bullets for independent points or numbered items for an ordered list.
